about.title: Oakland Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Getting hurt at work in Oakland rarely fits a tidy category. A fall from scaffolding, a forklift that backs up without warning, or a rear-end collision while making deliveries on I-880 can all leave you unsure who is responsible and what you can claim. California handles this in two lanes. Workers' compensation covers medical care and partial wage replacement through your employer, no matter who was at fault. It is usually your only remedy against the employer. But if someone outside your company played a part — a subcontractor, the owner of the property, the maker of a defective machine, or another driver on I-580 or International Boulevard — a separate injury claim may be available against that third party. Those claims can account for losses workers' comp does not, and they carry California's two-year filing window. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects injured Oakland and Alameda County workers with an independent attorney who can sort out which path, or both, fits your situation. No fee unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Oakland Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: We know where workers' comp stops
items.desc: Your employer's comp coverage is usually exclusive, but it does not shield a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or driver. The attorneys we connect you with look for that third party.

items.title: Deadlines are handled early
items.desc: You have 30 days to report an injury to your employer and two years to file a third-party claim in California. Getting connected promptly keeps both clocks from running out on you.

items.title: Retaliation is not something you have to absorb
items.desc: California law makes it illegal to fire, demote, or punish you for reporting a work injury. An independent attorney can address that alongside your injury claim, with no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I was hit on I-880 while driving a company vehicle in Oakland. Is that a work injury or a car accident?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were working, workers' compensation should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of who caused the crash. If another driver was at fault, you may also have a separate claim against that driver for losses comp does not cover. Oakland logged 2,054 injury collisions in 2025, many during commute and delivery hours, so this overlap comes up often here.

items.question: Can I sue my employer if the injury was clearly their fault?
items.answer: In most cases, no. California makes workers' compensation the exclusive remedy against your employer, even when the employer was careless. The exception is a negligent third party, such as a subcontractor on the same job site or the manufacturer of faulty equipment, who can be pursued in a separate injury claim.

items.question: What if I waited a few weeks to tell my supervisor I was hurt?
items.answer: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, so do it in writing as soon as you can. A late report can complicate a comp claim but does not automatically end it, and it does not affect the two-year deadline for a third-party claim. An attorney can help you document what happened and why the report came when it did.
